svg.aria-label: Diagram: how a Google Cloud organization policy inherits down the resource hierarchy, the difference between a constraint and a policy, the effect of inheritFromParent, why a denied value cannot be re-allowed by a descendant, and what applies when no policy is set anywhere
svg.title: Organization Policy inheritance: constraint versus policy, the hierarchy walk, and why denial wins
svg.text: IAM asks who. Organization Policy asks what.
A control that does not depend on the caller’s permissions cannot be escaped by escalating them.
Constraint — the blueprint
A particular type of restriction against a service,
published by Google. Does nothing on its own.
True for everybody. Implies nothing about you.
Organization policy — the building
Configures a single constraint. Set on an
organization, folder or project — nothing smaller.
All descendants inherit it by default.
The effective policy is computed, not stored — assembled from every ancestor
Organization
denies projects/123
Put denials here. They cannot be undone below.
Folder
inherits the denial
may add its own, may not remove one
Project
allows projects/123
Merged — DENY takes precedence.
Effective policy: denied.
The rules, in the order they decide
A policy set on a resource supersedes any policy set by its parents.
Real delegation — a project team can override what a folder decided.
inheritFromParent = true: the parent’s effective policy is inherited,
merged and reconciled into the result.
inheritFromParent = false: the resource does not inherit from its parent.
Detaches a whole subtree. Rarely what you want at a boundary you rely on.
For list rules, DENY values always take precedence.
Nothing set here? It inherits from the lowest ancestor that enforces one.
Nothing set anywhere above? The Google-managed default is enforced —
so an unset policy is not the same as an open one.
RestoreDefault returns the constraint’s default here, and children inherit it.
The asymmetry is the whole model
A parent can hand down freedom and have it refused. It cannot hand down a prohibition and have it ignored.
So design the hierarchy around denials: put them as high as they are true, because that is the only direction that holds.
Exceptions belong on a tag — constraints can be conditionally enforced on one. A label would do nothing.
Two timing facts that turn a five-minute change into an afternoon
Enforcement is usually not retroactive. A resource already in the forbidden state is in violation and keeps running.
Switching a constraint on closes the door. It does not undo the last hundred, and the console reconciles nothing.
Changes can take up to 15 minutes to be fully enforced — so wait and retry, and never stack a second edit.
